a:r.a:t: Complex Structures Are Stabilized by Non-Watson-Crick Base-Pair Interactions

p:cNvPr.descr: 3-dimensional structures of DNA. (a) Phenylalanine. The 3-D structure is on the left. It consists of green sugar backbones with blue, orange, red, and green. The structure is twisted in the double helix and bent to the right. To the right the connected phenylalanine structure is shown to the right. The phenylalanine is composed of cytosine (top), guanine (bottom), 7-methylguanine (right). The cytosine, to the top right, is a 6-sided ring structure. The structure consists of a box labeled ribose, bonded right to N. N bonds up and right to C, which double bonds right to C, which bonds down and right to C. C bonds right to N, which bonds up and down right to H. C double bonds down & left to N, which hydrogen bonds down and right to the H on the guanine, and left to C, which double bonds down and left to O. The O hydrogen bonds down and right to the H on guanine C then bonds up and left to the initial N. To the lower right is the guanine, labeled below. The guanine is a 2-ringed structure, consisting of a 6-sided ring structure bonded left to a 5-sided ring structure. For the 6-sided ring, the top right C double bonds up & right to O, down and right to N, which bonds down to C, which bonds down and right to NH2 and double bonds down and left to N. N bonds down to ribose (boxed), bonds left to C, which double bonds up to C, which bonds right to the initial O. This structure bonds right to the 5-sided ring, which contains N double bonded down and left to C, which bonds down and right to N. N bonds down and left to C (not shown) and right to C, which bonds up to C, which bonds up & left to C. To the upper right is the 7-methylguanine, which also consists of 2 rings. The 6-sided ring, on the left, begins with an N at the apex. N bonds down and right to C, which double bonds down to C, which bonds down & left to C. C double bonds down to O and up & left to N. N bonds up to C, which bonds up and left to N, which bonds left and right to H. H hydrogen bonds up to O, which is part of a phosphodiester bond with 2 ribose attached (pink). C double bonds right to the initial N. The 5-sided ring structure’s apical N bonds down and right to C, which double bonds down to N+. N+ bonds down and right to CH3, and left to C. C bonds up to C, which bonds right to the initial N. (b) Below this is the structure of a ribozyme. On the left is an illustration of the ribozyme, in which the helix, which has a green sugar backbone and red, orange, green, and blue bases, twists in a “hammerhead” shape. To the right is a close-up of the structure. It consists of adenine on the left and an N2-dimethylguanine on the right. The adenine consists of a ribose (boxed) bonded right to a 2-ring structure. The adenine has a 6-sided ring with 2 N and 3 double bonds, and a 5-sided ring with 2N and 2 double bonds. The bottom N of the 6-sided ring bonds left to C, which double bonds up to C, which bonds up and right to C, which bonds up to N, which bonds left and right to H. C double bonds down and right to N. N bonds down to C, which single bonds down and right to H and which double bonds down and left to the initial N. The double carbon bond on the left side is shared by the 5-sided ring. For the 5-sided ring, the top right C double bonds down to C, which bonds left to N, which bonds down and left to ribose, and up to C. C bonds up and left to H and double bonds up and right to N. N bonds down and right to the starting C. The H and N on the right side of the 6-sided ring hydrogen bond to an O and H, respectively, on the neighboring ring. To the right is the N2-dimethylguanine. It is a 2-ringed structure consisting of a 6-sided ring on the left and a 5-sided ring on the right. Beginning on the right is the ribose, which bonds left to the 5-sided ring. The ribose bonds left to N, which bonds up to C, which double bonds up and left to N. N bonds down & left to C, which bonds down to C, which bonds right to the initial N. Bonded to the left is the 6-sided ring. Beginning at the bottom, N bonds up and right to C, which double bonds up to C, which bonds up and left to C. C double bonds up to O and down & left to N, which bonds left to H and down to C, which bonds down to N. N bonds left and right to CH3. C double bonds right to the initial N. Below this image is the structure of an intron. On the left is the illustration, which resembled a strand of RNA tied in a knot. The green sugar backbones are looped and twisted around one another with the bases in the center. A particularly dense portion of the intron has the 2 sugar backbones and either side with a large mass of bases concentrated in the center, with no particular organization apparent. Bases are green, blue, red, and orange. To the right is the structure itself. It consists of an adenine (left) bonded right to a uracil (middle) which bonds down & right to a second adenine (right). The 2 adenines are flipped so that they are oriented in opposite directions (i.e., the left adenine is facing “up” and the right one is facing “down”). On the left, the adenine consists of 2 rings. On top is the 5-sided ring, bonded to the ribose. The ribose bonds down and right to N, which bonds up and right to C. C double bonds down and right to N, which bonds down and left to C, which double bonds left to C, which bonds up and left to N. Bonded directly below this is the 6-sided ring. The leftmost N bonds up and right to C, which double bonds right to C. C bonds down and right to C, which bonds right to N, which bonds up and down right to H. C double bonds down and left to N, which bonds left to C, which double bonds up & left to the initial N. The upper right N and one of the H atoms are hydrogen bonded to an H and O on the uracil to the right. To the upper right is the uracil. It is composed of a single 6-sided ring. The ring is bonded down and right to ribose. Ribose bonds up and left to C, which bonds down and left to C, which double bonds down to O and up & left to N. N bonds down and left to H and up to C. C double bonds up & left with O, and bonds up & right to C. C double bonds down and right to C, which bonds down to the initial C. On the other end of the ribose is a bond down and right to O, which bonds down and right to H. This is the ribose 2’ hydroxyl group, shown in pink and labeled 2’. The H hydrogen bonds down to the N in the adenine ring. The adenine ring has the same structure as previously described, but here the 6-sided ring structure is oriented upward, instead of downward.
